docs.b: fMRI brown bags The DBIC hosts a brown bag series featuring diverse topics in neuroimaging. These sessions provide opportunities to learn about emerging methods and receive feedback on ongoing projects. While most speakers are from the DBIC community, we occasionally invite speakers from the broader neuroscience field. The talks are typically held on Fridays at noon in Moore Hall, usually in person only, and typically for an internal (departmental) audience. They are announced via a mailing list; to join it, email Courtney Rogers. Visitors should ask her before attending. docs.t: History of the Dartmouth Brain Imaging Center (DBIC)
docs.l: Dartmouth has run a research-only MRI center since November 1999.
docs.b: Home History of the Dartmouth Brain Imaging Center (DBIC) In November of 1999, Dartmouth College became the first liberal arts school in the country to own and operate an MRI machine strictly for research. 1999 The DBIC opens under the direction of Scott Grafton, who directs it until 2006, with a 1.5T GE scanner. 2004 The DBIC upgrades to a 3.0T Philips scanner. 2006 Professor George Wolford serves as interim director in 2006 and 2007. 2008 Jim Haxby joins Dartmouth in January and directs the DBIC until June 2021. 2016 In August, the DBIC upgrades to its current Siemens 3T Prisma scanner. 2021 In July, the DBIC welcomes Tor Wager as its new director.

Research Scientist James (Jamie) Ford joined the DBIC in 2024. He leads an imaging group in the Acute to Chronic Pain Signatures (a2cps.org) project and helps develop the DBIC's processes for storing and processing MRI data, to ensure image quality and efficiency. Jamie has worked for more than 25 years in imaging centers at Dartmouth College, the Geisel School of Medicine, and Dartmouth Health. His past work and interests in imaging include structural, functional, and diffusion MRI, EEG, and NIRS, and he is available to provide guidance and technical support to research teams using the DBIC.

MRI Research Technologist Mike brings over twenty‑six years of MRI experience, most recently a decade at Dartmouth Health’s Advanced Imaging Center and Center for Surgical Innovation. He has extensive expertise in MRI safety, training, protocol development, data collection, and vendor collaboration. At the DBIC, Mike develops and runs the safety and operator training programs and helps research groups develop, implement and run their imaging protocols.

docs.l: Cancelling scan time close to the booking can carry a charge. This page sets out the policy and how to release time.
docs.h: Cancellation policy · Helping participants show up · How to cancel scan time
docs.b: Policies Cancellation policy Because demand for the scanner is high, the DBIC charges for scan time that is cancelled late. The policy applies to cancellations on or after Oct 1, 2021. You may be charged for scan time you book but do not use. If you cancel within the notice periods below, there is no charge. Cancellation policy When the time is released Charge More than 1 week before the session none Within 1 week (but more than 3 days) 50% Within 3 days 100% Helping participants show up To minimize cancellations, the DBIC asks researchers to: give participants the DBIC metal screener well before their scan; consider sending the DBIC information sheet, which lists things participants may not realize are an issue (for example non-removable piercings or certain hair and skin products); send an initial confirmation email, a reminder the week before, and a final reminder the day before the scan. How to cancel scan time Scan time should be released directly to Courtney Rogers by email.

docs.t: What is the DBIC’s cancellation policy?
docs.b: Booked time that is cancelled is still charged, though this charge will be reduced or waived with sufficient notice.

docs.l: The hourly rates for internally and externally funded studies, and how scan time is billed.
docs.h: Rates · How billing works · Questions
docs.b: Policies Scanning rates Rates Rates for scanning effective Jul 1, 2021. Internal funding means studies paid from Dartmouth-administered funds (for example a GL/PTAEO chart string). External funding means a non-Dartmouth funding source. Funding When Rate per hour Internal Peak hours (see scan hours) $500 Internal Off-peak hours, including weekends (see scan hours) $400 External Peak hours only (see scan hours) $700 How billing works Scan time is recorded in the DBIC logbook and billed on a monthly basis. The DBIC Associate Director for Operations (Courtney Rogers) emails an invoice for each DBIC protocol number (to the PI or designee) at the start of each month, covering the scans conducted in the previous month. The invoices list: scan dates, billing record, accession numbers, number of hours per scan, funding source, and the session cost for each scan. The PI (or designee) must review each invoice and verify that it is accurate. To request a correction, reply by the date given in the billing email. If Courtney Rogers does not hear back by that date, the invoice is treated as accurate and the account is charged. Questions Questions about billing or rates: contact Courtney Rogers.

Quick links Parking for non-Dartmouth DBIC participants Parking for Dartmouth-affiliated DBIC participants Unauthorized vehicle parking Non-Dartmouth research participant parking The DBIC has a dedicated parking spot located behind Moore Hall, reserved for non-Dartmouth research participants. If you have a non-Dartmouth participant who would like to use the parking spot for their visit, please request review and approval before your participant arrives (email Courtney Rogers, above). Then report the vehicle: Monday–Friday, 8 a.m.–4 p.m.: email Transportation Services with the date, time, make, model and license plate, and copy Courtney Rogers. Monday–Friday after 4 p.m. and all day Saturday and Sunday: call Safety & Security (603-646-4000) with the make, model and license plate.

Everyone who scans keeps the suite clean, tidy and ready for the next group.
docs.h: Housekeeping items · Equipment · The suite · Cleaning · At the end of the day
docs.b: Policies Housekeeping The MRI scanner and suite are a valuable shared resource. Beyond following all safety and operating procedures, scan operators must complete the full housekeeping checklist. The full checklist is the authoritative list; the items below are the ones most often missed. Housekeeping items Equipment Make sure the projector is in standby mode when not in use. Leave all peripheral equipment (BIOPAC, response devices, control box, video and sound systems) neat and untangled to avoid damage. Return corrective lenses to their appropriate slots in the storage case, and wipe down frames with a Clorox wipe. The suite Make sure no personal belongings are left in the scanner suite. Restock the scrub drawers. Place all used linens in the designated laundry bin. Make sure that all trash/recycling (including earplugs/earbuds, wrappers, used tape, etc.) have been disposed of in appropriate receptacles. Cleaning Wipe down all surfaces with frequent bodily contact (e.g. inside of the head coil, response pads, emergency squeeze ball) using the DBIC-provided Clorox wipes. At the end of the day Log out of REDCap and shut down the system when your lab is the last to scan that day.

docs.l: Becoming a certified scan operator takes two steps: first operator-in-training, then hands-on training and a competency demonstration.
docs.h: Step 1: Operator-in-training · Step 2: Certified scan operator · Skills at each step · What is expected of operators · Scheduling and class size
docs.b: Policies MRI operator training Prerequisite: MRI safety training The DBIC trains research faculty, postdoctoral fellows, graduate students, and full-time research staff to operate the scanner without an MRI Technologist being present. MRI operator training is a two-part process. The first step involves becoming an operator-in-training, and the second step is completion of the hands-on training required for operator certification. Important: All research personnel, including faculty, are required to remain current on all DBIC-mandated and institutional certifications relevant to MR safety and human subjects research. Personnel who do not actively participate in scanning activities for one academic year must repeat the DBIC MRI safety and operator trainings before resuming work in the scanning environment. Step 1: Operator-in-training To become an operator-in-training , you will need to book a training session; see How to book. During this training session, users will learn how to administer and follow all MRI safety scanning procedures, as well as be introduced to the skills listed under “Introduced in the first session” in Skills at each step. Step 2: Certified scan operator After the in-person introductory session, operators-in-training must complete at least 10 hours of hands-on training before they may use the MRI suite independently. The hours are scheduled according to the DBIC scheduling policies and must be completed under the supervision of a certified scan operator. They are recorded in an online training log, which you receive after the in-person operator training; the certified operator who supervises each session adds their initials to the log. The final competency demonstration involves independently running a scan study from start to finish, with a human participant, under the supervision of Mike Pearl, the MRI Technologist. The session can be booked according to the DBIC scheduling policies and must be run during normal business hours. To become a certified scan operator, researchers will need to demonstrate competence in the skills listed under “Demonstrated for certification” in Skills at each step. Skills at each step Each skill is introduced in the first session (Step 1) and demonstrated for certification (Step 2). Skill Introduced in the first session Demonstrated for certification MRI safety screening and the pre-scan checklist yes yes Metal detectors (handheld, pole) and their operating instructions yes yes Airlock door to the MRI suite yes yes Emergency procedures and incident reporting yes yes (thorough knowledge) Positioning participants in the bore yes yes Hearing protection (ear plugs/ear buds) yes yes Registering participants in REDCap yes yes Selecting and running a scan protocol yes yes, including checking the data transfer Powering the scanner on and off yes yes Stimulus and response devices — yes (independent set-up) DBIC logbook and scanner database entries — yes Housekeeping policies; Conducting research in the DBIC yes — MRUSER training manual yes (study the manual) yes (know its contents) What is expected of operators Scan operators must know and follow all DBIC safety policies and procedures at all times, and must follow the housekeeping policies that protect participants and equipment. Important: Non-compliance may result in the loss of independent scan operator privileges. Scheduling and class size Training is scheduled as needed, Monday–Friday between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. Classes are limited to 3 participants. How to book: To book the introductory session, or for questions about certification, email Courtney Rogers.

docs.b: Policies DBIC scheduling General info Scheduling tier descriptions Request windows, academic year 2026–2027 DBIC calendar Scheduling Courtney Rogers (Courtney.Rogers@Dartmouth.EDU) manages scheduling for all scanner activities. Email her to: request access to the Moore DBIC Scanner Outlook calendar, and submit your scan-time requests. The calendar can also be viewed online (see DBIC calendar below). When you request scan time, include your DBIC protocol number and the dates and times you would like. You will usually hear back within 1–2 business days after the request window closes. Scan hours Every session, in peak or off-peak hours, needs a certified scan operator and a scan buddy. Peak hours Monday–Friday, 8 a.m.–4 p.m. (the MRI Technologist’s working hours) Off-peak hours Monday–Friday after 4 p.m. All day Saturday/Sunday The MRI Technologist is not working during off-peak hours. Before you request time See the scanning rates. You need an approved DBIC protocol before you can request scan time; see how to submit a protocol. Scheduling tiers The DBIC uses a three-tier scheduling system. Requests within each tier are compiled and allocated by Courtney Rogers. Tier 1 Tier 2 Tier 3 Funding Grant-funded (external) DOF-funded All projects Booking opens on/around the first business day of the preceding month on/around the 8th of the preceding month on/around the 16th of the preceding month Stays open four business days four business days rolling, first come first served Share of time up to 60% the remaining 40% whatever is left Tier 1 – Grant-funded (external funding) Labs may request peak and off-peak time for the entire month. Up to 60% of weekly peak time (about 24 hours) and off-peak time (about 44 hours) may be allocated across all Tier 1 labs; the remaining 40% is reserved for Tier 2. Priority is based on project, with a maximum of two independent grant-funded projects per lab eligible for Tier 1 scheduling. Tier 2 – DOF-funded (Dean of the Faculty funding) Includes startup, dissertation and honors projects, and a lab's third and later projects. Priority is based on project, with up to two independent DOF-funded projects per lab eligible for Tier 2 scheduling. Tier 3 – All projects Requests are scheduled on a rolling, first-come, first-served basis. docs.h: Choosing a coil · The three coils
docs.b: Research Infrastructure Head coils The DBIC owns three phased-array head coils (64, 32 and 20 channels). Which one suits a study depends on what you need to measure and on who you scan. Choosing a coil The 64-channel head coil is the expected default choice: it is the newest design, has higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the cortex, and generally fits well, with some constraints. The 32-channel head coil has a more uniform SNR across the brain and a different fit. The 20-channel head coil is the roomiest, but the least advanced, particularly for modern parallel imaging. Two recommendations for any study: Explore at the start of the study which head coil meets your needs. Use only one head coil throughout a study, for consistency. The three coils Coil Signal-to-noise and imaging performance Fit 64-channel : the newest design, with 64 integrated preamplifiers. 40 of its 64 channels cover the head and the other 24 the neck. Higher SNR in the cortex: the small elements are much more sensitive close to the coil, so the SNR profile is weighted towards the cortex, more than with the other coils. The advantage does not reach deep structures, which may be imaged no better than with the 32-channel coil (it depends on the study). Suited to parallel imaging and simultaneous multislice (SMS). Generally good, and suits a wider range of participants than the 32-channel coil, including those who wear MR-compatible glasses. One particular fit constraint is in the neck. 32-channel : an earlier design with 32 integrated preamplifiers. A more uniform SNR across the brain, including deep structures. Suited to parallel imaging and simultaneous multislice (SMS). Tighter overall: participants with larger heads may not fit comfortably. Its fit constraints differ from the 64-channel coil's. 20-channel : the oldest design. The least advanced of the three, particularly for modern parallel imaging: it lacks the small receiver elements that improve compatibility with multiband imaging. The roomiest. It may be the only coil able to scan some participants with significantly larger heads.

docs.b: Research Infrastructure Computing DBIC systems access To use Discovery and other Research Computing systems, you need an HPC account (also known as a “Discovery account”). Everyone at Dartmouth has a NetID to provide authentication, but HPC access has to be set up before it will work: request it once, signing in with your NetID, at the HPC account request page. Research Computing creates the account and emails you when it is ready; it includes a 50 GB home directory on DartFS. For access to DBIC-specific resources (such as the shared datasets and our Discovery allocation) and for troubleshooting, we encourage you to contact DBIC directly, so that DBIC is in the loop: Courtney Rogers is the main contact point, and you can also write to Jamie Ford. Contacting Research Computing (research.computing@dartmouth.edu; this opens a support ticket) works too: Research Computing will typically either redirect these topics to DBIC or contact DBIC on your behalf, so DBIC may be involved in access decisions whether or not you realize it. DICOM scans Where scans appear DBIC scans appear on DartFS immediately after they are acquired at the scanner (see /dartfs/rc/lab/D/DBIC/DBIC/dbic-inbox/DICOM/ ), and are organized by date and accession. Access permissions are set based on the registered group nightly. If scans are resent from the scanner, note that: 1. Resent scans go to the same folder (based on date and accession) and will overwrite earlier versions if the series have not changed. If the series need to change, coordinate with DBIC or Research Computing to clear the earlier DICOM files before resending. 2. Scans resent after the day of acquisition do not trigger the automatic setting of access permissions; DBIC or Research Computing can trigger an update manually. Folders and accession numbers All MRI studies collected at DBIC are stored in the DICOM format, and organized according to acquisition date and an accession number that is intended to be unique. Thus a study recorded on Jul 4, 2019, with an accession number of A00001234 can be found on the server under the DICOM/ directory above at DICOM/2019/07/04/A00001234 . Always enter a unique accession value, even for test scans, because it determines where the scan is stored. A scan with no accession is stored as /unknown , and scans with a blank or generic accession (such as “test”) are at risk of colliding on DartFS if they are run on the same day. How the transfer works The DICOM files contain reconstructed MRI images obtained directly from the Siemens Console, which communicates with a dedicated virtual machine running a DICOM receiver (Orthanc). Orthanc carries out basic checking, maintains a temporary copy of scan data, and exports each DICOM to DartFS as it arrives. BIDS and DataLad DBIC has adopted the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) file-naming conventions for many recently acquired studies. BIDS is widely used in neuroimaging, and it supports data sharing, reproducible results and open science (Center for Open Neuroscience), principles the DBIC promotes. All DBIC investigators are encouraged to convert their data from DICOM to BIDS. All MRI data at DBIC is collected following ReproIn (NIH 1P41EB019936-01A1) convention. Researchers can also use the DataLad file-sharing and data-versioning utility (datalad.org). For technical details, including how to set up DataLad, see the DBIC Handbook (a user maintained resource that supplements this site). Storage (DartFS) DBIC's own scans and hosted datasets are on the DBIC share of DartFS: see DICOM scans and the Datasets page. Both the standard home directory quota and the free lab space below are set out in the Research Computing Bill of Rights. Your home directory Individual user accounts have a standard quota of 50 GB. This should be used for all code, writing, and anything that a user may need as they see fit. However, this space is not adequate for storing most datasets, and certainly not for multiple datasets. It is also insufficient for writing temporary files needed for complicated analyses and preprocessing. Lab space owned by your PI All Dartmouth faculty can request 1 TB of free storage for their lab's data. This space should be shared among lab members, and managed among those members by respective labs. Faculty members can buy more Lab-dedicated space as needs and resources demand and allow. Temporary scratch space There is a shared scratch space available to all users located at /dartfs-hpc/scratch that can be used as a workspace for analyses. Temporary files can sit there for long periods of time, and users will be notified by sysadmins before anything gets deleted. It is suggested that when processing data, users utilize this space as needed, and then copy a results folder (without intermediate products) to a permanent location, such as a home directory or lab directory. HPC (Discovery) Overview DBIC owns a share of the Research Computing (RC) Discovery cluster. RC's sharing policy gives share holders access to more than the resources they own, up to the limits shown below. The SLURM scheduler enforces these hard limits on resource allocation, so that once DBIC usage meets the limit, no more DBIC jobs can run until resources are freed. To ensure fair service for all DBIC users, the DBIC applies the policies below. RC system administrators implement and enforce them. Interactive nodes Access to the Discovery cluster requires an HPC account (see DBIC systems access); you then log on to an interactive node using SSH and your DartID credentials. Node Address Who can use it Use it for Discovery head node discovery7.hpcc.dartmouth.edu all Discovery users file handling and submitting jobs via SLURM; not for interactive jobs that need a lot of memory or multiple processors Ndoli ndoli.dartmouth.edu all DBIC users with Discovery access High memory system for testing code and interactive jobs Andes, Polaris andes.dartmouth.edu, polaris.dartmouth.edu all Discovery users High memory systems for testing code and interactive jobs DBIC users are encouraged to use Ndoli for testing code before submitting large jobs to the cluster. Individual user limits The SLURM job scheduler provides for specifying user limits for Trackable Resources (TRES), and all DBIC users have individual limits on TRES. This includes a hard limit of 240 cores that an individual can use at any time. docs.b: Research Infrastructure Public datasets hosted by DBIC Many public neuroimaging datasets are very large and hard to download one by one. To make them easier to use, the DBIC hosts selected datasets on the Dartmouth Research Computing file system, next to the Discovery cluster, where DBIC users can analyze them directly. Access. To navigate in the DBIC share on DartFS, you need to be in the rc-DBIC group (see DBIC systems access); most DBIC folders on DartFS cannot be reached without it. Each dataset’s “Access” line adds anything else that applies, such as dataset specific terms of use (where these exist, datasets require membership in an additional group, which is added once any requirements have been met). Some datasets are stored on Vast, a storage system separate from DartFS (their paths begin with /vast/ ), and are reached in the same way. List of hosted datasets Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC) Bissett Self-Regulation Dataset DBIC QA dataset HCP Young Adult HCP Lifespan: Aging and development Healthy Brain Network (HBN) ImageNet database Individual Brain Charting Life Narratives dataset Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) Spacetop The Moth 103 Tasks dataset Contact For questions about existing datasets or requests to add new datasets, please contact Jamie Ford (James.C.Ford@dartmouth.edu). Different datasets are administered by different people, so some entries give a different contact for access; for those, use the contact listed in the entry. DBIC QA dataset The Dartmouth Brain Imaging Center's QA data, converted to BIDS standard, can be accessed using the DataLad file-sharing and data-versioning utility (see the DataLad website). Path to DBIC QA data on Discovery: /dartfs/rc/lab/D/DBIC/DBIC/dbic-inbox/BIDS/dbic/QA Access: Open (no restrictions to rc-DBIC users) Online resources Clone of DBIC QA dataset - DataLad Repository Narratives dataset The Narratives Dataset is a large collection of fMRI studies in natural language processing conducted at Princeton Neuroscience Institute by the labs of Professors Ken Norman and Uri Hasson. The dataset consists of normalized 3T fMRI data collected while subjects (345 individuals) listened to various spoken word narratives with 28 unique stories and over 800 scanning sessions. This dataset is a benchmark for testing models of language processing and language comprehension. Path to the Narratives dataset on Discovery: /dartfs/rc/lab/D/DBIC/DBIC/archive/narratives Access: Open (no restrictions to rc-DBIC users) Online resources Nastase, S.A., Liu, YF., Hillman, H. et al. The “Narratives” fMRI dataset for evaluating models of naturalistic language comprehension. Sci Data 8, 250 (2021) Narratives Dataset - DataLad Repository Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) The Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) is a large ultra-high-field 7T fMRI dataset conducted by the Center for Magnetic Resonance Research at the University of Minnesota. It consists of high-resolution fMRI data collected from 8 adult subjects while they viewed thousands of images of natural scenes. Each subject was scanned multiple times with 30 to 40 sessions per subject. The NSD dataset is an excellent resource for testing models of visual representation and cognition. Path to the NSD on Discovery: /dartfs/rc/lab/D/DBIC/DBIC/archive/NSD . Access: Data Use Agreement (DUA) and group limited access permission Link to DUA: NSD data use agreement form Group limited access permission : Email Jamie Ford Online resources Natural Scenes Dataset website HCP Young Adult The Human Connectome Project (HCP) is a massive collaborative undertaking led by PIs Dr. David Van Essen of Washington University and Dr. Kamil Ugurbil of the University of Minnesota. The DBIC currently hosts the HCP Young Adult dataset, which contains 3T MRI data (structural, diffusion, resting-state and task fMRI) from over 1,100 healthy adults ages 22–35, in two forms: HCP1200 (original) and HCP-YA 2025 (released in 2025). Path to HCP YA datasets : /dartfs/rc/lab/D/DBIC/DBIC/archive/HCP/HCP1200 /vast/labs/DBIC/datasets/HCP-YA-2025 Access : Data Use Agreement (DUA) and group limited access permission Link to DUA : HCP Young Adult data use agreement (BALSA) note: same agreement and access applies to both versions Group limited access permission: Email Jamie Ford Information about the directory structure and file names: HCP1200 guide (PDF); HCP-YA 2025 release documentation. Online resources HCP Young Adult website Healthy Brain Network (HBN) The Healthy Brain Network (HBN) is a large 3T fMRI dataset conducted by the Child Mind Institute for developing human brains (ages 5–21). The whole study includes eye tracking, EEG and rich demographic and behavioral data that can be found on the HBN website. The data hosted by DBIC only includes the fMRI data. It consists of subjects under resting-state, eye-tracking calibration and watching two short movie clips ("Despicable Me" and "The Present"). We used the version from "Reproducible Brain Charts (RBC)" and the 845 subjects passing the quality check by the RBC team (up to "Release 9" by the HBN team). The paper on "Reproducible Brain Charts" can be found on ScienceDirect. In addition to the downloaded raw BIDS data and FreeSurfer 6 outputs, custom processing derivatives made with fMRIPrep and nb\ prep are included. Path to HBN dataset on Discovery : /dartfs/rc/lab/D/DBIC/DBIC/archive/HBN Access: Creative Commons (CC license) (open with restrictions) The HBN data uses a Creative Commons license with " BY-NC-SA " restrictions. BY (attribution) : citation requirements on eventual publications NC (non-commercial) SA (share-alike): if you reshare you must keep the CC restrictions Online resources Healthy Brain Network data descriptor (Scientific Data, 2017) Reproducible Brain Charts paper (ScienceDirect) Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC) The Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC) is a collection of three independent, open-access datasets—known as ID1000, PIOP1, and PIOP2—collected at 3T and totaling over 1,300 unique participants (N=928, N=216, N=226, respectively). Participants received T1-weighted, diffusion-weighted (DWI), and fMRI imaging. The functional data in the largest component, ID1000, is from movie watching of natural scenes by 19-26 year olds, while the two PIOP datasets include resting state and task-based fMRI of university students, with the latter targeting emotion matching and working memory (both), face perception, cognitive control, and emotion anticipation (PIOP1 only), and response inhibition (PIOP2 only). Demographics and psychometric variables are also included. The Amsterdam Open MRI Collection, a set of multimodal MRI datasets for individual difference analyses. Sci Data 8, 85 (2021). docs.l: A 3 tesla (3 T) Siemens MAGNETOM Prisma and the peripherals needed for functional neuroimaging.
docs.h: The system · Software and sequences · Hardware · Gradients · Magnet and shimming
docs.b: Research Infrastructure fMRI scanner The system Our center is equipped with a state-of-the-art 3 T Siemens MAGNETOM Prisma whole-body MRI system (Siemens Medical Solutions, Erlangen, Germany) and a variety of peripherals needed for functional neuroimaging. Software and sequences The scanner operates on the Siemens XA60 software platform. Vendor supplied packages are available for BOLD (Inline BOLD imaging, 3D PACE syngo and BOLD 3D Evaluation syngo), Diffusion (Diffusion Tensor Imaging, DTI Evaluation and DTI tractography syngo), and Spectroscopy sequences. Hardware Advanced hardware integration in our system (e.g. homogeneous 3 T magnet, XR 80/200 gradient system and transmission system) provide excellent B1 homogeneity, and enable novel capabilities such as simultaneous multislice (SMS) acquisition. Gradients On our system, the gradient rise time in all three axes is 200 T/m/s and peak gradient strength is 80 mT/m. Such a fast and powerful gradient system provides high-speed structural and functional imaging. Magnet and shimming Along with its uniform 3 T magnet, and capability of first and second order shimming, we can acquire high-quality MR spectra and images. The scanner's magnet delivers excellent magnetic homogeneity of 0.25 ppm, as measured within a 40 cm diameter spherical volume (DSV) in the 60 cm bore.

docs.b: Research Infrastructure Peripheral equipment General questions, requests for training, or technical support for any equipment listed here should be directed to: Michael Pearl (michael.a.pearl@dartmouth.edu). Menu Visual stimulation Auditory stimulation Participant response devices Eye tracking Physiological monitoring ReproStim Visual stimulation Panasonic PT-DW750BU projector The DBIC uses the Panasonic PT-DW750BU 7000-Lumen WXGA DLP Projector for the presentation of visual stimulus. This projector offers 7000 lumens of brightness and a 3000:1 dynamic contrast ratio, which work together to overcome light in most rooms and provide detail in dark areas of the image. Additionally, this projector has a WXGA 1280 x 800 native resolution for viewing detailed pictures or data. It is powered by a DLP chip system with a dual-lamp design. The PT-DW750BU includes a lens with a 1.8 to 2.5:1 throw ratio that can produce images from 50 to 600". The projector has HDMI, DVI-D, 5-BNC, and VGA inputs, which allows for different types of external video sources. It is controllable via Ethernet, RS-232, M3, or the included IR/wired remote control. The projector attaches to stimulus computer via video adapter. The image is mirrored on a monitor in the control room. Panasonic website DBIC user guide - projector Standing (out of bore) projection information Distances eye to mirror - 127mm mirror to screen - 1160mm screen to projector - 2032mm Image projection on the standing (out of bore) screen width- 428mm height - 266mm diagonal - 504mm Eyetracking (in-bore) projection information Distances eye to mirror - 127mm mirror to screen - 1010mm screen to projector - 2182mm Image project on the in-bore screen width- 475mm height - 297mm diagonal - 560mm Special note: If you are using the eyetracker (in-bore) screen, please reference the DBIC projector user guide to change the focus of the projector. MRIFocus (MRI-compatible corrective lenses) The DBIC uses Cambridge Research Systems MRIFocus for Siemens corrective lenses for both the 32- and 64-channel head coils. MRIFocus Kit Manufacturer's Users Manual DBIC userguide - MRIFocus kit Auditory stimulation Audio stimulus (Sensimetrics Model S14) The S14 insert earphones provide high-quality acoustic stimulus delivery while attenuating scanner noise. They are small enough to fit within any head coil, and can be covered with circumaural muffs for added protection if the coil allows. Frequency response equalization is achieved by pre-filtering stored digital stimuli. Equalization filters are provided and can be used either within Matlab or with a stand-alone filtering program (provided). A small power amplifier is required. Audio stimulus is connected to stimulus computer via 2.5mm jack. External speakers are available in the control room to allow monitoring of the audio stimulus. Sensimetric Model S14 website DBIC userguide - Sensimetrics Model S14 Participant response devices Current Designs 932 interface The opto-electronic interface receives optical signals from the handheld devices in the MR suite and converts them into electronic signals for the computer. The 932 is standards-based: the outputs are not designed to be used with a specific program or hardware platform, but are instead designed to work with everything. This interface provides complete USB, Serial, and Parallel outputs. Current Designs website DBIC user guide - Current Designs 932 4-button bimanual 2x2 Pyka 5-button grip Trackball 2 Joystick Optoacoustics FOMRI III microphone For recording verbal responses from participants during fMRI scanning, the DBIC offers the Optoacoustics FOMRI III microphone. Optoacoustics website DBIC Optoacoustics user guide Eye tracking SR Research EyeLink 1000 Plus The DBIC uses the SR Research Eyelink 1000 Plus for eyetracking data collection. Our system offers a high-speed camera with upgraded high-speed tracking, a fiber-optic camera head, long range mounting bar, 890nm Illuminator, 20/32/64 channel Siemens head coil mirror (16cm x 12cm), 50mm lens for MRI, and a Siemens Prisma tray mount. Installation guide for the EyeLink Developers Kit - macOS Installation guide for the EyeLink Developers Kit - Windows Eyelink user guide Physiological monitoring BIOPAC MP160 For collecting real-time physiological data during fMRI scanning, such as skin conductance, pulse rate, and respiration rate, DBIC maintains a BIOPAC MP160 system. The system includes a dedicated MacBook laptop running AcqKnowledge software facilitating data recording. A USB interface allows the investigator to connect their laptop to the BIOPAC system for synchronizing experimental and physiological time-courses, or for sending event markers or arbitrary time-course data. BIOPAC user guide ReproStim ReproStim is a video capture and recording suite for neuroimaging and psychology experiments, developed at the DBIC by Yaroslav (Yarik) Halchenko. Its goal is to provide experimenters with a complete record of audio and visual stimulation for every data collection session by making it possible to easily collect high fidelity copies of the actual stimuli shown to each subject in the form of video files that can be stored alongside behavioral or neuroimaging data in public repositories. ReproStim provides for enhanced experimental reproducibility and a safeguard against data loss in cases of data-collection irregularities. Because ReproStim provides an exact record of the actual stimuli delivered during any given experimental session, it makes it possible to precisely reproduce experimental sessions, even if the original trial sets were randomized and precise trial details not recorded. In cases of experimental irregularities, such as aborted fMRI runs, unexpected glitches in trial timing, or programming errors that cause records of trial conditions to be lost, valuable data (which can be especially costly in cases of fMRI of ECog, for example) can be recoded and recovered using the audio-visual record provided by ReproStim. The developmental version of ReproStim is currently deployed at the DBIC and we are archiving video of the stimuli shown during every scanning session (not video of participants). The computer called ReproIner runs the ReproStim software at the DBIC. For more information, contact Yaroslav Halchenko or check out ReproStim on GitHub

docs.h: Overview · 32-channel head coil · 64-channel head coil · Weekly QA metrics · Weekly QA reports · 2026 · Phantom
docs.b: Research Infrastructure QA Overview Weekly metrics Weekly QA reports Phantom Overview QA metrics using the tools created by the Function Biomedical Informatics Research Network (fBIRN) are generated on weekly basis to monitor stability of the scanner. These scans run a standardized fMRI protocol executed on an agar phantom using the DBIC's 32- and (since 2018) 64-channel head coils. Details of the FBIRN protocol can be found on the NITRC fBIRN project page and in the references below. Longitudinal results for mean ghost percentage, signal-to-fluctuation-noise ratio (SFNR) and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) are updated here weekly. Abnormalities in any of the metrics may indicate instability of some hardware component, and such abnormalities are investigated. In addition, the Siemens customer QA tool is run to check coil elements of the head coil (weekly) and body coil (monthly) and as needed. The acceptable mean ghost percentage is less than 3% (ref. 2). The first QA on DBIC's Siemens Prisma was conducted on Sep 12, 2016. 32-channel head coil 64-channel head coil Weekly QA metrics Below are definitions of the metrics found on the DBIC's weekly QA report. Definitions have been adopted from the original authors. Signal image - the mean signal across time Signal summary value - the mean across the ROI of the signal image Standard Deviation Image (Temporal Fluctuation Noise Image) - voxel by voxel residuals of second-order polynomial fit across SNR - the signal value (‘mean’) divided by the image standard deviation; provided as a summary value (using mean across the ROI of the static spatial noise image) and as an image SFNR - calculated voxel-by-voxel across a 21×21 ROI in the center of a phantom after removing a second-order polynomial trend from each voxel's time course; the mean signal image is divided by the standard deviation of the detrended residual image (provided as a summary value using the average across the ROI and as an image) Percent fluctuation - 100\ std/msi where 'std' is a summary value calculated as the standard deviation of the residuals of a second-order polynomial fit of the time series and 'msi' is mean signal intensity of the time-series. Drift - 100\ (maxroi-minroi)/msi where 'maxroi' and 'minroi' are the maximum and minimum values of the mean raw signal over the ROI. Driftfit - 100\ (maxfit-minfit)/msi where 'maxfit' and 'minfit' are the maximum and minimum values of the fit. Fourier Analysis (Magnitude Spectrum) - the frequency spectrum resulting from a Fourier analysis of the residual data. Radius of Decorrelation (RDC) - a measure of the size of ROI at which statistical independence of the voxels is lost. Smoothness (Full-width Half-maximum) - calculated using the AFNI tool 3dFWHMx Center of mass - a simple mean intensity of each volume, with each voxel's value weighted by its index in the X, Y, or Z direction. Odd-Even Difference Static Noise Image - created by subtracting the sum of even-numbered time-series frames from the sum of odd-numbered frames, and captures static noise (thermal/electronic) Mean Ghost Percentage - 100\ meanGhost/meanSignal. The ghost metrics are calculated for each volume by taking a dilated mask ("original mask") of the data, and shifting it by N/2 voxels in the appropriate axis to create a "ghost mask". The mean intensities of those voxels in the original mask and not in the ghost mask ("meanSignal") and of voxels in the ghost mask and not in the original mask ("meanGhost") are calculated. References: 1. Friedman L, Glover GH. Report on a multicenter fMRI quality assurance protocol. J Magn Reson Imaging. 2006;23(6):827-839. PubMed: 16649196 2. docs.b: Research Infrastructure Sequences Mainstream sequences, including functional (BOLD), diffusion, anatomical (T1w, T2w, T2-FLAIR), spectroscopy, and angiography are available for use. Available sequences Vendor supplied sequences come from Siemens; the others have been installed here. Kind of scan Vendor supplied Installed (CMRR or custom) Settings (PDF) Functional MRI (BOLD) : brain activity, from blood-oxygenation changes ep2d bold cmrr mbep2d bold (also used for multi-echo fMRI ) BOLD; Multi-echo fMRI Diffusion : the diffusion of water, used to map white-matter pathways ep2d diff; qDWI (q-space diffusion weighted) cmrr mbep2d diff Diffusion Spectroscopy : the chemical content of a chosen region csi se; csi slaser MEGA-PRESS (custom-installed) Angiography : blood vessel mapping phase contrast (PC) and time of flight (TOF) Anatomical (T1w, T2w, T2-FLAIR) : brain structure mprage (T1w); T2w and T2-FLAIR sequences Field mapping : magnetic-field uniformity, used to correct image distortion field-mapping sequences Spin-echo EPI cmrr mbep2d se All of these sequences can be customized (for example slice thickness, repetition and echo times, or turning filters on and off) to suit each researcher’s needs. Simultaneous multislice (SMS) Simultaneous multislice (SMS, also called multiband or MB) acquires several slices at once, so data can be collected faster. It can be used with either the vendor supplied BOLD and diffusion sequences or the CMRR versions that are installed. Multi-echo fMRI This allows multiple images to be collected at different echo times (TEs) after a single excitation pulse, improving data quality and analysis options, though at the cost of analysis complexity and longer acquisitions (TRs). It is provided by the CMRR BOLD pulse sequences. CMRR sequences The CMRR sequences are modified versions of the vendor supplied BOLD and diffusion pulse sequences, made by CMRR at the University of Minnesota. They give more flexibility to customize protocols. More about them: CMRR multiband instructions (PDF).
